title: Alignment Goals in Adult Spinal Deformity Surgery
condition_or_topic: Sagittal alignment goals in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery
clinical_background: An aging population, a high prevalence of ASD among people older than 60 years, and demand to maintain independence have contributed to increased ASD surgery. Earlier surgical goals emphasized alignment measures associated with disability and health-related quality of life (HRQL), particularly sagittal rather than coronal measures. Although surgical quality metrics have improved, mechanical complications remain the leading reason for readmission and unplanned reoperation. Alignment planning has therefore shifted from population-based regional targets toward individualized segmental goals that also address mechanical complications.
objectives: Review current concepts and goals for sagittal alignment in ASD surgery, including their relationships with HRQL and postoperative complications.
Examine the strengths and weaknesses of different alignment strategies and identify the principal areas of debate.
study_design: Narrative review of publications on sagittal alignment concepts and surgical alignment goals in adult spinal deformity (ASD).

population.description: The review concerns adults with ASD; the authors did not enroll a patient cohort.

interpretation: The authors consider postoperative alignment relevant to mechanical complications after adult spinal deformity surgery, although no available alignment strategy reliably eliminates mechanical failure or reoperation. They argue that correction should address spinal shape, curvature distribution and magnitude while resolving compensatory postures. The influence of alignment on health-related quality of life is less consistent across studies, potentially because conventional alignment targets and patient-reported measures do not adequately capture individualized alignment and function.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The SRS-Schwab classification established outcome-associated radiographic targets, but its emphasis on SVA and PI-LL does not fully represent compensation or spinal shape, and mechanical complications remain common even in patients meeting its goals. Lafage et al proposed age-adjusted targets and subsequently associated smaller postoperative PI-LL mismatches with PJK; however, later validation has not consistently shown better outcomes using those thresholds. Roussouly-based restoration has been associated with fewer mechanical complications when the intended shape is achieved, while the GAP score has produced mixed external-validation results; a cited systematic review reported a global AUC of 0.68 ± 0.2 across eleven retrospective articles. In a cited analysis of 247 adults, deviation in either direction from the T4-L1-Hip Axis targets was associated with greater mechanical-complication risk, but the authors regard external validation as insufficient.
clinical_implications: Undercorrection may sustain pelvic retroversion and opposing forces around the upper end of a fusion construct, potentially increasing PJF risk; tension in the lower lumbar construct may also favor pseudarthrosis.
Excess lumbar correction may produce negative global sagittal alignment and lead to pelvic anteversion or, more commonly, proximal junctional kyphosis.
Malalignment may contribute to adjacent-segment degeneration, particularly after shorter fusions.
Age-related changes in alignment may reflect spinal degeneration rather than age itself, so age alone may not adequately define an individual's correction target.
Reciprocal adjustment after surgery depends on mobility in unfused spinal segments; it is not expected in conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis.
practice_implications: Evaluate segmental, regional and global alignment for the individual patient rather than relying only on average age-related values.

Consider restoration of the lower lumbar arc, appropriate placement of the lumbar apex and an upper lumbar arc suited to PI, while avoiding overcorrection and excessive posterior tilt at the inflection point.
Plan carefully for spinal harmony and horizontal gaze when reciprocal changes cannot be expected.

Consider the patient's spinal morphology, symptoms, expectations, health and comorbidities when individualizing correction and balancing its potential benefits against the risks of a more aggressive operation.
limitations: The authors identify selection, performance and collider biases in retrospective cohort evidence on alignment strategies.
Patient-specific fusion potential and surgeon-specific proximal exposure techniques cannot be adequately accounted for in the statistical analyses discussed, complicating interpretation.
Exploratory regression findings may be misinterpreted when model quality is not assessed.

The SRS-Schwab classification does not account for age or spinal shape and uses fixed levels to assess LL; validation against mechanical failure is difficult because its development relied on patient-reported outcomes.
The Roussouly classification divides patients into categories despite PI varying continuously.
The GAP score does not incorporate the thoracic region.

Most alignment strategies do not incorporate TK or C2 Tilt, and several proposed targets, including SVA, GT and TPA, reflect compensation or reciprocal change rather than variables directly controllable during surgery.
The T4-L1-Hip Axis approach remains relatively new and lacks sufficiently robust external validation.
open_questions: Whether a fused spine should have the same ideal alignment as an unfused spine remains unresolved.
It is disputed whether older patients should routinely receive less correction and retain more positive sagittal malalignment and pelvic retroversion.
The long-term consequences of fusing a younger adult to age-adjusted targets over 20, 30, or 40 years are unknown.
How best to assess sagittal alignment across the available methods remains debated.
future_directions: Further investigate alignment targets that restore spinal shape, distribution and magnitude while eliminating compensatory mechanisms.
Develop individualized correction goals that account for spinal morphology, symptoms, expectations, health and comorbidities.
Pursue stronger external validation of T4-L1-Hip Axis targets in adult spinal deformity surgery.
Examine patient-related factors not adequately addressed in existing research, including biology, genetics and -omics, as potential contributors to postoperative complications.
Explore whether large patient cohorts and advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence can support more complex individualized alignment models.

tables.title: Comparison of strategies for achieving spinal alignment goals
tables.summary: The table contrasts whether each strategy uses PI or age adjustment, which alignment measures it specifies, and whether the cited literature supports prediction of HRQL or mechanical complications and external validation. It marks SRS-Schwab as age-adjusted, although the article’s discussion says that classification did not account for age.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that strategies for planning alignment in adult spinal deformity surgery have improved, but mechanical failures and repeat operations remain concerning. They favor further investigation of individualized goals that restore spinal shape, distribution and magnitude while eliminating compensatory mechanisms; the optimal targets remain disputed.
narrative_summary: This narrative review examines sagittal alignment concepts and surgical targets in adult spinal deformity, focusing on health-related quality of life and postoperative mechanical complications. The authors explain that conventional measures, including PI-LL and SVA, may not adequately characterize spinal shape or compensatory pelvic and lower-limb posture for an individual patient. They compare SRS-Schwab, Roussouly-Laouissat, GAP, T4-L1-Hip Axis and segmental approaches. In a study cited by the review, mechanical complications occurred in 72% of surgical patients whose postoperative shape did not match the intended Roussouly type, versus 15% of those whose shape matched. Another cited study of 247 adults undergoing long fusion identified 68 (27.5%) with mechanical complications; deviation in either direction from its proposed L1PA or T4-L1PA alignment was associated with higher risk. The authors also report mixed external validation of GAP, while a cited systematic review found a global AUC of 0.68 ± 0.2. These findings support attention to both the magnitude and distribution of correction, rather than a single regional measure. However, the review emphasizes that retrospective-study biases complicate interpretation, mechanical complications persist even after apparently appropriate alignment, and T4-L1-Hip Axis still needs stronger external validation. The authors consider individualized goals important, while leaving unresolved whether targets for a fused spine should match those for an unfused spine and how age should influence correction.

subgroup_analyses: Across cited studies, LL changed relatively little until roughly the age of 70, whereas decreases were observed beyond age 70, particularly on reaching 80 years of age. Other reported alignment measures increased with age; the authors caution that spinal degeneration, rather than age itself, may explain loss of sagittal alignment.

For older patients with greater sagittal deformity (PI-LL >30°), cited studies described less contribution from thoracic hypokyphosis and pelvic retroversion to compensation, with greater contributions from knee flexion and pelvic shift.

Roussouly type 1 has SS <35° and a lumbar apex at L5; type 2 has SS <35° and an apex at L4; type 3 has SS between 35 and 45° and an apex at L4; type 4 has SS >45° and an apex at L3 or higher. Type 3 AP, added in 2018, describes hyperlordosis with low-grade PI and very low or negative PT in an anteverted pelvis.

Lafage et al proposed age-specific targets ranging from PT = 10.9°, PI-LL = 10.5°, and SVA = 4.1 mm for patients < 35 years to PT = 28.5°, PI-LL = 16.7°, and SVA = 78.1 mm for patients > 75 years. The review notes that subsequent validation has not consistently shown improved outcomes using these thresholds.

In a later study, Lafage et al found smaller postoperative PI-LL mismatches in patients with PJK than in patients without PJK; middle-aged and older patients with PJK were overcorrected relative to age-specific thresholds.

The GAP age modifier uses age ≥60. GAP classifies scores of 0-2 as proportioned, 3 to 6 as moderately disproportioned, and 7 to 13 as severely disproportioned, categories associated with increasing mechanical complication rates.

Pesenti et al reported L1-2, L2-3, L3-4, L4-5 and L5-S1 segmental lordosis of 1.4°, 5.7°, 9.4°, 14.6°, and 20.2°, respectively, in patients with mean PI of 39.1° (low PI); 2.3°, 7.7°, 11.6°, 16.2° and 20.5°, respectively, with mean PI of 51.7° (average PI); and 4.9°, 10.8°, 14.4°, 16.5° and 19.4°, respectively, with mean PI of 68.6° (high PI).
secondary_results: Bernhardt and Bridwell reported segmental lumbar lordosis of 4° at L1-2, 7° at L2-3, 13° at L3-4, 20° at L4-5 and 28° at L5-S1 in a model that did not account for pelvic parameters. Their thoracic measurements reached 5° at each level between T4 and T9, with an inflection point at T12-L1.

The review describes insufficient correction as potentially maintaining pelvic compensation and increasing forces that may contribute to PJF or pseudarthrosis. Excessive lumbar correction may instead lead to pelvic anteversion or proximal junctional kyphosis. These are proposed mechanical relationships, not quantified event comparisons in the review.

The review reports mixed evidence for GAP external validation and states that T4-L1-Hip Axis still lacks sufficiently robust external validation despite having been tested in two adult deformity databases.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: This narrative review examines sagittal alignment concepts and surgical goals in adult spinal deformity (ASD). Surgical planning has shifted from population-average regional targets toward individualized segmental targets, and from goals based only on health-related quality of life (HRQL) toward goals that also address mechanical complications. Traditional measures, including pelvic incidence - lumbar lordosis (PI-LL), thoracic kyphosis and sagittal vertical axis (SVA), may be insufficiently specific for individual planning. Pelvic retroversion and knee flexion help maintain upright posture. Evidence relating postoperative sagittal alignment to HRQL improvement has been conflicting; limited sensitivity of conventional alignment targets and patient-reported measures may contribute to that conflict. Recent studies suggest that sagittal parameters have limited effects on HRQL scores in nonoperated patients but significantly affect postoperative HRQL and mechanical complications after spinal fusion. Current evidence favors resolving compensatory mechanisms and restoring an appropriate spinal shape to reduce postoperative mechanical complications. Several strategies pursue those goals. Despite advances in alignment planning over the last decade, mechanical failure and reoperation remain concerns; this review examines the approaches, their limitations and the principal disagreements.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Population aging, the desire to remain independent without major disability and the high prevalence of ASD above 60 years of age have contributed to a marked rise in ASD surgery. Initial work sought alignment features associated with impaired HRQL and disability. Sagittal measures correlated most strongly with HRQL, whereas coronal measures had a limited role. Although quality measures for ASD surgery improved over the last decade, mechanical complications remain the leading reason for readmission and unplanned reoperation. Understanding alignment and pursuing individualized postoperative targets are associated with fewer postoperative mechanical complications. Over 20 years, goals have evolved from population-based regional averages to patient-specific segmental alignment and from HRQL alone to prevention of mechanical complications. The review aims to present recent insights into these issues.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a narrative review of publications addressing sagittal alignment concepts and goals in ASD surgery. They summarize alignment philosophies and their reported relationships with HRQL and postoperative complications.

document_sections.heading: Normal Spinopelvic Alignment Cone of Economy and Measures of Sagittal Alignment
document_sections.content: Dubousset’s ‘Cone of Economy’ describes upright sagittal postures maintainable with minimal energy use. Positions outside that range require compensation and greater energy expenditure. Spinal alignment, pelvic tilt and lower-limb alignment determine an individual’s position within it. Global sagittal alignment describes the static overall spinal shape and the relative positions of the head, spine and pelvis. “Sagittal Balance” concerns whether the spine is in equilibrium and is often considered dynamic. Appropriate alignment permits energy-efficient upright posture; malalignment may require compensatory activity to preserve it.

document_sections.heading: The Pelvis.
document_sections.content: Pelvic incidence (PI) is the angle relating the sacral endplate to the femoral-head centers. It indirectly characterizes pelvic morphology and underpins assessment of spinopelvic alignment. PI rises gradually during childhood with anterior-posterior pelvic growth and is nearly stable in adulthood, apart from sacroiliac nutation or counternutation averaging 2-3 degrees in adults. PI also appears to change in patients with bilateral pelvic fixation as a compensatory response. Across studies, adult median PI lies between 50° to 55° (IQR between 45° to 60°). Some US-centered studies report racial variation, but the finding is inconsistent. Sacral slope (SS) specifies sacral-endplate orientation relative to the horizontal; pelvic tilt (PT) describes sacral orientation relative to the hips in standing. Their geometric relationship is PI = PT + SS. Both relate strongly to PI, but the relationship is complex: people with the same PI can have a wide range of normal PT, making a normal PT or SS defined strictly from PI potentially misleading.

document_sections.heading: Regional Sagittal Alignment.
document_sections.content: Studies generally agree on normative lumbar alignment. Historically, PI and lumbar lordosis were treated as linearly related, and PI-LL mismatch became an important measure of sagittal balance and a guide to deformity correction. Later work describes a more complex relationship. Several studies find little association between L4-S1 lordosis and PI; median L4-S1 lordosis is near 35° (IQR between 25° to 50°). L1-S1 lordosis has a weak, nonlinear relationship with PI (r2 ∼ 0.3), and an approximate normal estimate is LL = PI x 0.6 + 30°. Its normal range can extend up to ± 20°, and its total angle does not show how lordosis is distributed. Likewise, simple lordosis and kyphosis angles do not characterize spinal shape. L1 pelvic angle relates more strongly to PI; a normal estimate is L1PA = 0.5 × PI – 21°. Roussouly’s study of asymptomatic people described 4 lumbar shapes distinguished by SS and by the lengths and magnitudes of upper and lower lordotic arcs. The lower arc runs from S1 to the lumbar apex, the most anterior lumbar point touching a vertical line; the upper arc runs from that apex to the thoracolumbar inflection point where lumbar lordosis becomes thoracic kyphosis. Geometrically, the lower arc equals SS, while the upper arc is relatively stable in magnitude at ∼18° but varies in length. Subsequent understanding treats normal sagittal shape as a continuum rather than separate categories. Vertebral pelvic angles (VPAs) offer an alternative to sagittal Cobb angles: they characterize spinal shape and its position relative to the hips, including pelvic version. Mathematically, they represent a spinal spline with vertebral-body points as knots. VPAs show excellent within-observer and between-observer reliability, with measurement error typically less than 2°; numerous studies advocate their use. Hills et al studied 320 MEANS volunteers without radiographic degeneration, deformity or a history of spinal pathology. They described the ‘T4-L1-Hip Axis’ through the relationships of L1PA with PI (r2, 0.58) and T4PA with L1PA (r2, 0.81). Their results indicate that 80% of the population have an L1PA corresponding to the stated normal PI-based relationship and a T4PA within 4° of L1PA. Equality of T4PA and L1PA places the T4-to-hip line through the L1 centroid. They also found a weak, nonlinear PI relationship for L1-S1 lordosis (r2=0.3) and PI-independent L4-S1 lordosis, with a median of 37° and a normal range of 25° to 55°, rather than a single constant value. Their findings accord with increasing upper-arc lordosis as PI rises. VPAs more strongly reflect PI and global alignment, have lower measurement error, represent curvature distribution and become fixed after fusion to the sacrum. The description of sagittal shape also notes equal magnitudes for the lower lumbar arc and SS, and for the upper lumbar and lower thoracic arcs.

document_sections.heading: Global Sagittal Alignment.
document_sections.content: Several measures characterize global sagittal alignment or balance. C7 Sagittal Vertical Axis-SVA is the distance from the C7 plumb line to the posterior superior S1 endplate. Its principal usefulness is following the same patient over time: pelvic tilt changes do not affect it, so C7 SVA can measure 0 mm in either a normal spine or a maximally compensated posture. It also varies with PI, limiting comparisons between patients. Several studies favor C2 tilt, also called the Odontoid-Hip-Axis, as a measure of global sagittal balance. It is independent of PI and varies little in normal individuals; its median is 2.7° (IQR, 4.4 to 1.1). Geometrically, C2 tilt = PT + C2PA. A normal C2 tilt likely provides an objective indication of balance within the cone of economy; in well-balanced people, PT will therefore be nearly equal to C2PA within the relative limits of PT. C2 tilt is defined by the line from the odontoid center to the bicoxofemoral axis relative to a vertical line through that axis. C2PA, T4PA and L1PA are vertebral pelvic angles defined using a vertebral centroid, the center of the superior S1 endplate and the bicoxofemoral axis.

document_sections.heading: Degeneration of Normal Alignment and Age
document_sections.content: Table 1 presents normative radiographic values from healthy MEANS volunteers with a median age of 37 years; alignment changes with advancing age. Reports generally find little change in LL until roughly the age of 70, followed by reduced LL beyond age 70 as lumbar degeneration develops, especially at 80 years of age. Most studies report age-related increases in TK, PT, SVA, T1 pelvic angle (TPA), global sagittal alignment (GSA), global tilt (GT) and T1 Tilt. Nonetheless, full-body alignment measured from the auditory-meatus center and a force-plate gravity line can remain stable because adjacent spinal regions, hips and knees compensate. MEANS volunteers used slight pelvic retroversion, knee flexion and neck extension to keep the skull centered over the knees. Although studies describe more kyphotic alignment with age, the authors consider spinal degeneration a potentially more accurate explanation for lost sagittal alignment. Degeneration correlates with age, but an older person without degeneration would not necessarily have increased TK; age may therefore confound rather than directly cause the change. Individualized surgical goals require assessment of segmental, regional and global alignment instead of reliance solely on average age-related changes.

document_sections.heading: Compensatory and Reciprocal Changes in ASD
document_sections.content: Sagittal malalignment may progress to imbalance. The energy cost of maintaining upright posture through compensation can cause fatigue. Compensation begins with greater lordosis in adjacent spinal segments, then proceeds through pelvic retroversion, hip extension, pelvic shift, knee flexion and finally ankle dorsiflexion. In older patients with larger deformities (PI-LL >30°), thoracic hypokyphosis and pelvic retroversion contribute less, while knee flexion and pelvic shift contribute more. Most surgical realignments are expected to resolve compensatory activity. After correction, unfused spinal segments and lower limbs may change reciprocally to accommodate the new alignment. Klineberg et al observed increased TK after lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) in patients without thoracic fusion, consistent with the Roussouly relationship between the upper lordotic arc and lower thoracic kyphotic arc. Thoracic PSOs similarly corrected preoperative hyperlordosis. These responses require mobility in the unfused spine; they are not expected in conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis, so planning must account for spinal harmony and horizontal gaze. Table 1 summarizes normative radiographic parameters in the 320 international asymptomatic MEANS volunteers without prior spinal disease or surgery. Positive sagittal malalignment may produce cervical hyperlordosis that improves after lumbar PSO; after thoracic PSO, this response may be less evident because the lumbar region may undergo more reciprocal change than the cervical region. If surgical alignment targets are missed, reciprocal changes may worsen malalignment. Lafage et al found an unexpected TK increase that worsened SVA and PT in more than one-half of lumbar PSO cases whose upper-most instrumented vertebra (UIV) was below T10. This finding was linked to older age, greater preoperative sagittal malalignment and higher PI. They proposed that insufficient correction, increased spinal loading and greater muscle atrophy might explain it.

document_sections.heading: Impact of ASD
document_sections.content: ASD commonly causes severe functional disability and back pain. Early univariate studies identified positive correlations between sagittal spinopelvic measures and HRQL scores in ASD, although r2 values were low, suggesting greater disability with malalignment. Beyond the deformity’s physical and mental effects, degeneration can cause neurological dysfunction and disabling back pain refractory to nonsurgical care. Heterogeneity in ASD contributes to substantial variation in both surgical and nonsurgical management. In operated patients, Takemoto et al found that post-fusion sagittal spinopelvic parameters remained significantly associated with postoperative Oswestry Disability Index-ODI after covariate adjustment. Restoring physiological alignment is consequently a goal in most surgical plans.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Realignment Goals in ASD
document_sections.content: Alignment strategies seek to understand normal spinal parameters. The approaches discussed are the Roussouly classification, SRS-Schwab classification, age-adjusted goals, GAP score, T4-L1-Hip Axis and segmental alignment restoration.

document_sections.heading: Roussouly.
document_sections.content: Failure to restore the lordotic shape and arc distribution described by the Roussouly classification has been associated with mechanical complications. Its original 4 types came from young asymptomatic people and were distinguished by SS and lumbar-apex location: type 1 has SS <35° and an L5 apex; type 2 has SS <35° and an L4 apex; type 3 has SS between 35 and 45° and an L4 apex; and type 4 has SS >45° and an apex at L3 or higher. A fifth pattern, type 3 AP, was added in 2018 and features hyperlordosis, low-grade PI, and very low or negative PT with pelvic anteversion. Lower subtypes have a lower inflection point and fewer lordotic vertebrae; higher types have a higher inflection point and more lordotic vertebrae. Reported interobserver reliability ranges from 0.4 to 0.68. Recognizing the type may help select the appropriate inflection point. Pizones et al reported mechanical complications in 72% of surgical patients whose postoperative shape did not match the ideal Roussouly type, versus 15% when it did.

document_sections.heading: SRS-Schwab Classification.
document_sections.content: Schwab and colleagues used regression models to identify spinopelvic thresholds associated with ODI >40, described as moderate disability: PT >22°, SVA >47 mm and PI-LL >11°. These thresholds informed the Scoliosis Research Society-Schwab (SRS-Schwab) classification and were later proposed as surgical alignment goals. Schwab et al associated larger PI-LL mismatch, higher PT and higher SVA with worse scores. The classification does not incorporate age or spinal shape and uses fixed levels to determine LL. Because its development relied on patient-reported outcomes, of which alignment is only one component, validation against mechanical failure has been difficult. Nonetheless, it emphasized appropriate alignment and its relationship with PI and prompted further alignment-outcome research.

document_sections.heading: Age-Adjusted Alignment Targets.
document_sections.content: Lafage et al proposed age-adjusted goals to make the SRS-Schwab framework more patient-specific. Their regression models related preoperative alignment and HRQOL to age-specific targets for PT, PI-LL, SVA and T1PA. Proposed values rise with age, from PT = 10.9°, PI-LL = 10.5° and SVA = 4.1 mm for patients < 35 years to PT = 28.5°, PI-LL = 16.7° and SVA = 78.1 mm for patients > 75 years. In a subsequent study, Lafage et al found smaller postoperative PI-LL mismatches in patients with PJK than in those without it; middle-aged and older patients with PJK were also considered overcorrected by age-specific thresholds. This emphasized potential harm from overcorrection as well as undercorrection. However, because targets were derived from outcome scores rather than mechanical failures, validation studies have not consistently shown better outcomes at those thresholds. Degeneration is associated with both aging and spinal malalignment and may be an important confounder.

document_sections.heading: Global Alignment and Proportion (GAP) Score.
document_sections.content: The Global Alignment and Proportion (GAP) Score was introduced to estimate mechanical-complication risk and guide alignment after ASD reconstruction. It includes an age modifier defined by age ≥60 and divides patients into three groups with increasing mechanical-complication rates. Like Roussouly-based targets, it uses PI to individualize goals from a single preoperative measurement. It also uses Global Tilt (GT), which combines C7 Vertical tilt - C7VT, the angle relating the C7 plumb line to a line between the centers of C7 and the superior S1 endplate, with PT: GT = C7VT + PT. The score incorporates age, PI, SS, L1-S1 lordosis and L4-S1 lordosis. Deviations from ideal alignment are characterized in 4 domains: relative pelvic version-RPV, relative lumbar lordosis-RLL, Lumbar distribution index-LDI and relative spinopelvic alignment-RSA. Scores of 0-2 indicate proportioned alignment, 3 to 6 moderately disproportioned alignment and 7 to 13 severely disproportioned alignment. External validations have yielded mixed findings. A cited systematic review of eleven retrospective articles reported a global AUC of 0.68 ± 0.2, interpreted as moderate predictive accuracy for mechanical complications.

document_sections.heading: T4-L1-Hip Axis.
document_sections.content: Hills et al derived the T4-L1-Hip Axis from volunteers without spinal deformity or degeneration. Its 2 components are a PI-related normal L1PA, stated earlier as L1PA = 0.5 × PI – 21°, and a T4-L1PA mismatch near 0°; at that mismatch, the line from T4 to the hips crosses the L1 centroid. T4PA is measurable during surgery and becomes fixed after instrumentation from the sacrum to T4. In a study of 247 adults undergoing long fusion from the upper thoracic spine to the sacrum, 68 (27.5%) had mechanical complications, defined as radiographic PJK, displaced rod fracture, or revision for PJK or pseudarthrosis. After adjustment for age, deviations from normal L1PA or T4-L1PA mismatch in either the overcorrected or undercorrected direction were associated with greater mechanical-complication risk. Risk was lowest within normal alignment. Age was not associated with mechanical-failure risk in that analysis. Greater departure from normal sagittal alignment was also associated with worse HRQOL at 1 year after surgery. Potential advantages include continuous rather than categorical targets, intraoperative measurability of both T4PA and L1PA, and their stability after long instrumentation to the sacrum. Further external validation is needed.

document_sections.heading: Segmental Alignment Goals.
document_sections.content: Bernhardt and Bridwell described normal thoracic and lumbar segmental parameters without accounting for pelvic measures. Their lumbar model increases caudally: lordosis is 4° at L1-2, 7° at L2-3, 13° at L3-4, 20° at L4-5 and 28° at L5-S1. Thoracic kyphosis peaks at 5° at each level between T4 and T9, then decreases toward neutral cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junctions; their kyphosis-to-lordosis inflection point is T12-L1. Although individual segmental magnitudes may depend on PI, this distribution provides a template for bending rods in most constructs. Pesenti et al described PI-related segmental alignment. They reported approximately constant L4-S1 lordosis of 35° irrespective of PI, whereas L1-L4 lordosis increased with PI. For mean PI of 39.1° (low PI), L1-2 through L5-S1 lordosis was 1.4°, 5.7°, 9.4°, 14.6° and 20.2°, respectively; at mean PI of 51.7° (average PI), corresponding values were 2.3°, 7.7°, 11.6°, 16.2° and 20.5°; at mean PI of 68.6° (high PI), they were 4.9°, 10.8°, 14.4°, 16.5° and 19.4°. A cohort undergoing degenerative 1 to 3 level fusions supported the 35° L4-S1 target: patients who attained distal lordosis goals had fewer adjacent-level degeneration events and revisions. Lai et al defined cranial SVA hip (CrSVA-H) as the distance between the femoral-hip center and a vertical line from the skull’s nasion-inion midpoint. In their 363-patient ASD series, multivariable regression identified CrSVA-H as a significant independent predictor of 2-year SRS-22r scores. They recommended using CrSVA-H rather than C7 SVA as a postoperative sagittal target.

document_sections.heading: Limitations to Current Alignment Strategies and Areas of Controversy
document_sections.content: The best way to assess sagittal alignment among available approaches remains disputed; Table 2 compares the strategies, their targets, HRQL and mechanical-complication prediction, and external validation. Retrospective cohorts are vulnerable to selection, performance and colliding biases. Patient-specific biological fusion potential and surgeon-specific proximal exposure technique cannot be adequately controlled statistically, complicating interpretation. Exploratory analyses may also be interpreted without checking model quality, leading to unsound conclusions from regression equations. Nevertheless, postoperative alignment appears relevant to mechanical complications. With undercorrection, compensatory pelvic retroversion can direct forces dorsally at the UIV while forces on unfused spine act ventrally; their convergence may raise PJF risk. Ventral forces may also place the instrumented construct, particularly the lower lumbar region, under tension rather than compression and favor pseudarthrosis. Malalignment may additionally promote adjacent-segment degeneration, especially after shorter fusions. Conversely, excessive lumbar-lordosis correction generally produces negative global sagittal alignment, prompting pelvic anteversion or, more commonly, proximal junctional kyphosis as the body seeks a C2 Tilt of 0°. Meeting SRS-Schwab targets has been associated with better HRQL and fewer mechanical complications, but mechanical-complication rates remain high even in patients considered well aligned. Its emphasis on SVA, which misses compensation, and PI-LL overlooks lordotic shape and distribution. Roussouly identified regions of high spinal stress and the importance of an appropriate lumbar distribution index (LDI); insufficient lower lumbar lordosis or flat back increases disc stress. A limitation of Roussouly and other categorical classifications is that PI varies continuously. GAP quantifies individualized shape and distribution through relative pelvic version, relative LL, lordosis distribution index and relative sagittal alignment, but omits the thoracic region. Roussouly et al and GAP developers described a distribution range of 50% to 80% in aligned cases and linked LDI together with relative LL to mechanical failure. Laouissat et al described reciprocal relationships between sacral orientation and sagittal shape: an undercontoured rod induces pelvic retroversion, whereas an overcontoured rod produces postoperative hyperlordosis and iatrogenic pelvic anteversion. The T4-L1-Hip Axis may advance assessment of both curvature distribution and magnitude, but despite testing in two adult-deformity databases, it remains novel and lacks robust external validation. Most strategies omit TK or C2 Tilt. Some proposed goals, including SVA, GT and TPA, cannot be directly controlled intraoperatively because they largely express compensation or reciprocal change. Considering how spinal curves interact, the authors emphasize restoring the lower lumbar arc, locating the lumbar apex appropriately and extending the upper lumbar arc according to PI without overcorrection or excessive posterior tilt of the inflection point.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions and Areas for Future Research
document_sections.content: Understanding of ideal spinal alignment has advanced, but disagreement persists. It is uncertain whether an ideal fused-spine alignment should match that of an unfused spine: an unfused patient does not face fusion-related mechanical failures and can use unfused segments for compensation. The authors question whether all older patients should receive less correction and retain greater positive sagittal malalignment and pelvic retroversion. Applying age-based targets could leave otherwise well-aligned older patients fused in malaligned positions. The long-term consequences for a younger adult fused to age-adjusted targets after 20, 30, or 40 years are also unknown. Increasingly individualized ASD care recognizes that age or any other single factor cannot define ideal alignment. Understudied patient factors, including biology, genetics and -omics, may contribute to postoperative complications. The authors consider normalization of spinal shape, distribution and magnitude, together with elimination of compensatory mechanisms, an important subject for future study. Ideal correction may need to account for spinal morphology, individual symptoms and expectations, and the patient’s capacity to tolerate correction given health and comorbidities. Patient-specific goals may help balance the benefits and risks of more aggressive correction. Modeling these factors will likely require many patients and may benefit from machine learning and artificial intelligence.
